title: Printing in the US
one_liner: A mature manufacturing industry where digital substitution keeps legacy print shrinking, while direct mail, labels, packaging, signage and short-run digital work provide pockets of demand.
overview: The industry prints on paper, apparel, plastic, metal, glass and other materials using lithographic, flexographic, gravure, screen, digital and letterpress processes, excluding publishers that print for themselves and standalone prepress or postpress shops. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline characterized the industry as declining, with revenue at $79.7 billion and long-run losses in advertising inserts, catalogs, forms, newspapers and magazines. Current public data through 2025-2026 point to the same structure: total printed volume continues to migrate to digital channels, employment keeps falling, but shipment values are steadier because prices, packaging-adjacent work, direct mail, in-store marketing, signage and personalized short-run digital printing offset part of the physical-volume decline.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 manufacturers' value of shipments for printing was $88.2 billion, calculated from Census/FRED monthly not-seasonally-adjusted NAICS printing shipments totaling $88,161 million in 2025; this is a public current proxy and is broader than the 2022 IBIS NAICS 32311 revenue baseline.
key_stats.growth: 2025 shipments grew 0.6% from $87.7 billion in 2024, while BLS reported NAICS 323 output fell 2.3% in 2024 and hours worked fell 2.7% in 2025, indicating price/mix support rather than broad real-volume growth.
key_stats.employment: BLS reported NAICS 323 employment of 341,000 in May 2026, down from the 2022 IBIS baseline of 421,417 employees.
key_stats.establishments: BLS QCEW reported 27,525 private NAICS 323 establishments in Q4 2025; Census Business Patterns reported 21,354 employer establishments for NAICS 32311 printing in 2023.
key_stats.prices: BLS reported the NAICS 323 producer price index at 182.608 in May 2026, up 0.6% month over month.
key_stats.direct_mail: USPS Marketing Mail volume was 56.8 billion pieces in FY2025, down from 57.5 billion in FY2024, while revenue rose to $15.7 billion in FY2025.

baseline_2022.market_size: $79.7 billion revenue in 2022, in 2022 dollars, from the baseline IBISWorld file.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue increased 1.8% year over year after declining at a 2.9% CAGR over 2017-2022.
baseline_2022.profit: $3.4 billion profit in 2022, equal to a 4.3% margin.
baseline_2022.outlook_from_baseline: IBISWorld forecast 2022-2027 revenue decline at a 2.5% CAGR to $70.3 billion by 2027.

how_it_makes_money: Printers earn revenue from commercial lithographic, flexographic, screen, gravure and digital printing; book and publication printing; advertising inserts, catalogs and direct mail; forms, checks and transactional documents; labels, packaging, signage, in-store marketing, apparel decoration and custom print-on-demand work. Larger operators increasingly bundle print with mailing, logistics, data, creative, media, workflow automation and marketing execution services to protect account relationships as print volumes decline.
cost_structure: The cost base is dominated by paper, substrates, ink, plates, energy, equipment, labor, finishing, warehousing and outbound logistics. In 2022, industry wages were $19.9 billion, about 25.0% of IBIS baseline revenue, and profit margin was 4.3%. Quad's 2025 results illustrate large-printer economics: cost of sales was 78.4% of net sales, SG&A was 13.5%, depreciation and amortization was 3.2%, and operating income was 4.0%. BLS reported average hourly earnings for NAICS 323 at $31.18 in May 2026, with production and nonsupervisory earnings at $25.02.
major_players: Quad/Graphics Inc. - 2025 net sales of $2.4 billion, with US Print and Related Services accounting for about 92% of consolidated net sales.
R.R. Donnelley & Sons Company - private global provider of marketing, packaging, print and supply-chain solutions; acquired Williams Lea in 2025 to expand business services.
Cimpress plc - FY2025 revenue of $3.403 billion globally, led by Vista, PrintBrothers, signage, packaging and labels growth.
Deluxe Corporation - 2024 checks accounted for 33.1% of consolidated revenue, exposing the company to long-term payment digitization.
Taylor Corporation - private print, marketing communications and packaging group with broad US commercial-print exposure.
CJK Group / LSC Communications - book, catalog, magazine and publication-printing operator serving publishing and education markets.
current_dynamics: The market is no longer just losing pages to the internet; it is being remixed toward fewer, more targeted, more automated jobs. Advertisers still use direct mail and in-store print when physical media can cut through crowded digital channels, but run lengths are shorter, jobs are more data-driven, and customers expect fast turnaround and integrated fulfillment. Legacy newspaper, magazine, directory, check and business-form work continues to decline. Printers with scale, mailing infrastructure, CRM data integration, packaging capabilities and automated digital presses are better positioned than small generalists dependent on commodity offset volume.
whats_growing: Growth is concentrated in personalized direct mail, election-cycle and nonprofit mail, labels, packaging, signage, in-store marketing, short-run digital print, print-on-demand, web-to-print ordering, data-driven campaign execution and outsourced publishing fulfillment. Cimpress reported FY2025 growth in Vista product categories including signage, packaging and labels, and Quad highlighted strong 2025 performance in targeted print, direct mail, packaging and in-store marketing.
whats_shrinking: Shrinking categories include newspaper and magazine advertising inserts, long-run publications, directories, checks, business forms, retail catalogs, undifferentiated offset jobs and low-value print products that can be replaced by email, apps, online statements, e-commerce listings or digital ads. USPS OIG's 2025 baseline scenario projects combined First-Class and Marketing Mail volume down 29% from 2025 to 2035, reinforcing the long-run pressure on mail-related print volume.
recent_developments: 2025-01-31: RRD finalized its acquisition of Williams Lea, expanding from print and packaging into tech-enabled business services.
2025-06-02: USPS OIG projected First-Class and Marketing Mail volume could decline 14% to 41% from 2025 to 2035, with a 29% baseline decline.
2025-11-14: USPS reported FY2025 Marketing Mail revenue of $15.7 billion and volume of 56.8 billion pieces, with volume down 1.3% from FY2024.
2026-02-17: Quad reported 2025 net sales of $2.4 billion, down 9.4% from 2024, or down 4.8% excluding its European divestiture impact.
2026-02-25: FRED's full 2025 not-seasonally-adjusted printing shipments series showed $88.2 billion in annual shipments, up 0.6% from 2024.
2026-06-16: BLS reported May 2026 NAICS 323 employment of 341,000 and a producer price index of 182.608.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is flat-to-down in real terms. Nominal shipments can hold near the high-$80-billion range if pricing, packaging, labels, direct mail and signage remain resilient, but employment, establishments and physical print volumes are likely to keep declining. Winners will be printers that combine automation, variable-data digital print, mailing intelligence, omnichannel marketing services and packaging or specialty substrates. The main risks are accelerated electronic substitution, continued decline in periodicals and checks, postal-rate increases, tariff and substrate-cost shocks, and weak customer advertising budgets.
themes: Paper, ink, labor and postal-cost pressure
data_year: 2025-2026 current data, with 2022 baseline from the provided IBISWorld file
one_sentence: US printers remain under structural pressure from online advertising, e-commerce workflows and paper-cost volatility, but 2025 shipment data show the market has stabilized around the high-$80-billion range when broader NAICS 323 printing and support shipments are used as the current public proxy.

title: Printing, Paper, Food, Textile & Other Machinery Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A fragmented machinery niche where food-processing automation is offsetting weaker printing, paper and textile equipment demand.
overview: This industry covers specialized industrial machinery used by food and beverage processors, paper and wood-product plants, printers, textile producers and other manufacturers. The baseline IBISWorld report put 2022 revenue at $31.028 billion in 2022 dollars, after a 2.2% annualized increase from 2017 to 2022. By 2025, a reasonable baseline-derived revenue estimate is about $32.3 billion in 2022 dollars using the report's 1.4% annualized 2022-2027 outlook, while the broader NAICS 33324 industrial machinery proxy recorded $39.942 billion of 2025 sectoral output in current dollars. Demand is cyclical because customers buy machinery when they expand, modernize or replace lines, but it is uneven by segment: food and beverage machinery is benefiting from automation, sanitation, inspection and protein-led production trends, while printing and textile machinery remain pressured by digitization, imports and offshored apparel supply chains.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated industry revenue: about $32.3 billion in 2022 dollars; broader NAICS 33324 sectoral output was $39.942 billion in 2025 current dollars.
key_stats.growth: 2022-2027 baseline forecast CAGR: 1.4%; broader NAICS 33324 sectoral output rose 1.2% in 2025 versus 2024 and 0.6% CAGR from 2022 to 2025.
key_stats.food_processing_machinery: 2025 US food and beverage processing machinery shipment value: $6.2 billion, up 3.2% from 2024, with a forecast of $6.7 billion by 2027.
key_stats.baseline_profit_margin: 2022 EBIT margin: 3.7% of revenue, equal to $1.148 billion of profit on $31.028 billion of revenue.
key_stats.broader_machinery_conditions: Machinery manufacturing employment was 1.084 million in June 2026, with average hourly earnings of $38.97; machinery manufacturing PPI reached 198.238 in June 2026.
key_stats.orders_indicator: Industrial machinery new orders were $4.317 billion in May 2026, versus $4.566 billion in April 2026 and $4.271 billion in January 2026.
key_stats.capacity_indicator: Machinery manufacturing industrial capacity index was 115.609 in Q2 2026, compared with 115.503 in Q4 2025.

baseline_2022.exports: $3.282 billion in 2022, equal to 10.6% of revenue.
baseline_2022.imports: $9.022 billion in 2022, equal to 24.5% of domestic demand.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 product mix: food product machinery 34.0%, all other industrial machinery 29.4%, paper industry machinery 15.9%, printing machinery and equipment 15.1%, textile machinery 5.6%.

how_it_makes_money: Companies generate revenue by designing, fabricating and assembling specialized machinery, integrated production lines, controls, replacement parts and retrofit packages for manufacturers. Large capital projects are often quoted and delivered to customer specifications, while recurring revenue comes from aftermarket parts, maintenance, field service, software, controls upgrades and rebuilds. Food and beverage processors, snack producers, protein processors, paper converters, printers, textile producers and machinery wholesalers are key customer channels.

cost_structure.materials_and_components: 2025-2026 cost exposure remains high because machinery producers buy fabricated steel, stainless steel, bearings, motors, drives, controls, electronics and machined components; AISI reported 2025 steel imports down 12.6% year over year and finished steel import share at 18%, pointing to tighter import supply conditions for some metal buyers.
cost_structure.labor: 2022 wages were $6.795 billion, or about 21.9% of industry revenue; broader machinery manufacturing average hourly earnings were $38.97 in June 2026.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 EBIT margin was 3.7%, with baseline forecast improvement to 4.2% by 2027 if steel and other input pressures ease.
cost_structure.overhead: Other costs include engineering, plant overhead, depreciation, warranty reserves, freight, installation crews, sales channels, software and R&D for automation, sanitation, inspection and controls.

major_players: JBT Marel Corporation - major food and beverage processing equipment supplier after completing the Marel acquisition on January 2, 2025.
ProMach - private processing and packaging machinery platform active in food, beverage, pet care, labeling, coding and end-of-line automation.
BW Packaging / Barry-Wehmiller - packaging machinery and integrated line supplier serving food, beverage, household, medical and industrial customers.
Kadant Inc. - supplier of process, fiber, wood-processing, material-handling and flow-control equipment tied to paper, recycling and industrial processing markets.
Duravant - private automation equipment platform serving food processing, packaging and material handling applications.
Heidelberger Druckmaschinen and Koenig & Bauer - global printing press suppliers competing in the US printing equipment market.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is split between stronger food, beverage, packaging and automation demand and weaker capital spending in paper, print and some wood/fiber-linked niches. Customers are still replacing aging equipment, especially in snack and packaged-food plants, and are prioritizing throughput, sanitation, labor savings, inspection and connected controls. At the same time, higher financing costs through 2025, tariff uncertainty, imported equipment competition and volatile steel/component pricing are keeping many buyers selective. Public data show broader NAICS 33324 output nearly flat from 2022 to 2025, but food processing machinery grew 3.2% in 2025 and remains the best-supported subsegment.
whats_growing: Food and beverage processing machinery, with 2025 US shipment value of $6.2 billion and a 2027 forecast of $6.7 billion.
Automation retrofits, robotic handling, inspection systems, AI-enabled monitoring and predictive maintenance as manufacturers address labor shortages and uptime targets in 2025-2026.
Snack, prepared food, pet food, protein, dairy and hygienic processing equipment, led by product variety, single-serve formats and higher sanitation expectations.
Aftermarket parts, service and modernization work as customers defer some large projects but keep existing lines running.
End-of-line packaging and integrated automation partnerships, including 2025-2026 activity by ProMach and BW Packaging.
whats_shrinking: Printing machinery tied to newspapers, office documents and other formats displaced by digital media and paperless workflows.
Textile machinery demand linked to domestic apparel production, which remains constrained by offshore supply chains despite reshoring interest.
Paper and fiber capital equipment in markets exposed to mill closures, excess capacity or weak housing-linked wood demand in 2025.
Commodity or less-differentiated machinery exposed to cheaper imports and customer price sensitivity.
Large discretionary capital projects where customers delayed orders in 2025 because of tariffs, trade uncertainty and financing costs.
recent_developments: 2025-01-02: JBT completed the Marel acquisition, creating a larger global food and beverage technology equipment supplier.
2025-01-09: PMMI reported 88% of surveyed snack food makers intended to acquire new machinery by 2027, with 57% of purchases replacing older equipment.
2025-09-30: Census published 2024-2025 monthly shipments and new-orders data for industrial machinery manufacturing, highlighting the sector's order-cycle volatility.
2026-02-19: AISI reported full-year 2025 US steel imports fell 12.6% from 2024 and finished-steel import market share was 18%.
2026-05-08: PMMI and FPSA reported the US food and beverage processing machinery market reached $6.2 billion in 2025 shipments, up 3.2% from 2024.
2026-07-02: Census reported May 2026 total manufacturing shipments rose 1.6% while total new orders fell 1.3%, showing mixed near-term capital-goods momentum.
outlook: The industry should grow slowly rather than break out. Food and beverage processing, packaging automation, inspection and aftermarket service should keep expanding through 2027, but printing, paper and textile machinery will remain mature or declining. Baseline revenue is expected to rise from $31.028 billion in 2022 to about $33.3 billion in 2027, a 1.4% CAGR in 2022 dollars. Upside comes from lower interest rates, reshoring, automation spending and food safety investment; downside comes from metal prices, tariffs, a strong dollar, weak print demand, delayed mill projects and import competition. Operators with proprietary equipment, controls software, installed-base service networks and sanitation/automation expertise are positioned better than firms selling standardized machines.

one_sentence: US manufacturers of food, paper, printing, textile and other specialized industrial machinery sell capital equipment, parts and service into downstream manufacturing markets, with 2025 demand supported by food automation, replacement cycles and broader equipment investment but restrained by weak legacy print/paper uses, cautious capital budgets and metal-cost volatility.

title: Private Banking Services
one_liner: Private banks advise, manage and lend against the wealth of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients.
overview: The US private banking industry serves individuals and families with investable assets generally above $1.0 million, with more intensive services for ultra-high-net-worth households, family offices and entrepreneurs. Core demand is tied to HNW population growth, public-market performance, private-market access, estate planning complexity, liquidity events and cross-border wealth flows. After the 2022 baseline of $83.1 billion in revenue, newer market estimates put the US private banking revenue pool at $112.5 billion in 2025 and about $120.6 billion in 2026, implying a materially larger market than the pre-2022 forecast. Growth is being supported by 2025 gains in US millionaire counts, strong 2025 equity returns, demand for alternatives and securities-based lending, and digital-advice investments, while fee pressure, compliance costs and advisor talent competition restrain margins.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: $120.6 billion estimated US private banking revenue; 2025: $112.5 billion reported market revenue
key_stats.growth: 2026: 7.2% estimated revenue growth based on 2026-2031 CAGR; 2025: US private banking market revenue $112.5 billion
key_stats.private_client_assets: 2025: $37.4 trillion in estimated US private-client assets
key_stats.us_hnwi_population: 2025: 8.7 million US HNWIs in Capgemini data, up 9.2% from 2024
key_stats.profitability_context: 2025: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management pre-tax margin was 29.3%; 2022 IBIS industry profit margin was 39.2%

baseline_2022.source: IBISWorld baseline file, last updated Jun. 26, 2022

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes mainly from percentage-of-assets advisory and management fees, trust and estate administration fees, custody and account fees, brokerage and structured-product commissions, performance or carried-interest-linked fees on some alternative strategies, net interest income from deposits and private-client loans, securities-backed lending spreads, mortgage and credit products, foreign-exchange and transaction charges, and family-office retainers.
cost_structure: The largest costs are advisor and relationship-manager compensation, bonuses and recruiting packages, technology platforms, portfolio and risk systems, compliance and AML/KYC controls, office and client-service infrastructure, custody and clearing, investment research, insurance, legal costs, and corporate overhead. Scale improves margins because advisory platforms, research, compliance and technology can be spread across larger AUM, but 2025-2026 pressure is rising from AI investment, cyber controls, AML scrutiny and competition for elite advisor teams.
major_players: JPMorgan Chase: 2025 Asset & Wealth Management revenue of $24 billion, $7.1 trillion in client assets and 4,101 Global Private Bank client advisors
Morgan Stanley: 2025 Wealth Management net revenues of $31.8 billion, 29.3% pre-tax margin and $356 billion net new assets
Bank of America Merrill/Private Bank: 2026 company disclosure of about $4.9 trillion in client balances across wealth management businesses
UBS: 2025 annual report shows major global wealth management scale after Credit Suisse integration; 2026 reports cited $4.94 trillion in invested assets in Q2
Goldman Sachs Private Wealth Management/Apex: focused on UHNW, family-office, alternatives and capital-markets access
Northern Trust, Citi Private Bank, Wells Fargo Private Bank, BNY Mellon Wealth Management, Rockefeller Capital Management and large independent RIAs compete in UHNW and family-office segments
current_dynamics: Demand is strong because wealthy US households benefited from 2025 equity-market gains, AI-linked wealth creation, private-company liquidity events and rising use of alternatives. Pricing is mixed: AUM growth supports fees, but large clients negotiate harder, passive products pressure portfolio-management fees and independent RIAs compete aggressively. Banks with lending, deposits, tax, estate, capital-markets and family-office capabilities have an advantage over stand-alone advisors. Compliance intensity remains high in AML, sanctions, beneficial ownership, cybersecurity, conflicts and private-fund disclosure.
whats_growing: Alternative investments, private credit, secondaries, private equity access, tax-aware direct indexing, family-office services, philanthropy advisory, estate and succession planning, securities-backed lending, concentrated-stock monetization, digital onboarding, AI-supported advisor workflows and advice for entrepreneurs after IPOs or private-company liquidity events are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Traditional brokerage commissions, branch-centric service models, cash sweep economics versus peak-rate periods, generic balanced portfolio mandates, smaller undifferentiated private-bank teams, manual compliance workflows and standalone product-pushing models are losing share to integrated advice, platform scale and fiduciary planning.
recent_developments: 2025-01: SEC charged LPL Financial with AML failures and announced an $18 million penalty, reinforcing compliance risk for wealth platforms.
2025-06: Capgemini reported the US added 562,000 HNWIs in 2024 to reach 7.9 million, supporting 2025 private-bank client growth.
2025-07: FinCEN announced plans to delay the investment adviser AML rule effective date from Jan. 1, 2026 to Jan. 1, 2028.
2025-08: SEC staff changed review practices for registered closed-end funds investing in private funds, easing some historical accredited-investor and 15% private-fund comment positions.
2025-10: RBC and Campden reported North American family offices were expanding AI use and that private markets represented 29% of average family-office portfolios.
2026-06: Capgemini reported US HNWI population reached 8.7 million in 2025, up 9.2%, while global HNWI wealth rose 8.7% to $98.3 trillion.
outlook: The industry outlook is positive through 2026 because HNW wealth, private-client assets and demand for complex planning continue to rise. Revenue should grow faster than the 2022 IBIS forecast if public markets remain constructive and liquidity events continue, with 2026 market revenue estimated near $120.6 billion. Risks include equity-market reversals, lower net interest margins, compressed advisory fees, regulatory enforcement, tax-policy uncertainty, cybersecurity losses and advisor attrition. The strongest operators will combine balance-sheet lending, tax and estate expertise, alternatives access, global custody, AI-enabled service and high-touch relationship management.
one_sentence: Private Banking Services generate recurring advisory, asset-management, trust, estate-planning, lending and transaction revenue from affluent clients whose portfolios expanded with 2025 equity gains, alternative-asset allocations and continued US wealth creation.

title: Private Detective Services
one_liner: Private detective firms sell fact-finding, surveillance, background-screening and fraud-investigation work to employers, insurers, law firms, government clients and consumers.
overview: Private Detective Services covers NAICS 561611 investigation and detective services, including private investigations, background checks, skip tracing, polygraph and fingerprinting services, but excluding guard, patrol and armored-car services. The baseline IBIS report put 2020 revenue at $6.3 billion after a COVID-19 decline and projected recovery to $7.3 billion by 2025. Public Census/FRED data show employer-firm investigation services revenue reached $7.850 billion in 2022, up 8.6% from 2021, implying the industry recovered faster than the 2020-vintage baseline expected. For 2025, a reasonable current estimate is about $8.5-$8.7 billion for employer-firm investigation services, assuming low-single-digit annual growth from the 2022 Census benchmark, supported by higher 2025 corporate profits, steady legal demand, continued screening volume and rising fraud complexity.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated employer-firm revenue: $8.5-$8.7 billion; latest official Census/FRED benchmark: $7.850 billion in 2022
key_stats.growth: 2022 revenue growth: 8.6% year over year from $7.229 billion in 2021; 2025 estimated growth: low single digits
key_stats.employment: BLS OOH: private detectives and investigators held about 43,600 jobs in 2024; employment projected to grow 6% from 2024 to 2034
key_stats.pay: BLS OOH: median annual wage was $52,370 in May 2024
key_stats.openings: BLS OOH: about 3,900 private detective and investigator openings per year projected over 2024-2034
key_stats.profitability: IBIS baseline forecast: 2025 EBIT margin of 7.3%, up from 5.2% in 2020

baseline_2022.market_size: $7.850 billion employer-firm investigation services revenue in 2022, Census/FRED
baseline_2022.growth: 8.6% year over year in 2022 versus $7.229 billion in 2021
baseline_2022.context: 2022 revenue was 28.9% above the 2020 Census/FRED level of $6.088 billion, reflecting a sharp post-pandemic rebound

how_it_makes_money.revenue_model: Operators charge hourly, per-case, subscription, retainer or contract fees for background checks, surveillance, field investigations, skip tracing, litigation support, SIU and insurance claims work, due diligence, public-record searches and fraud investigations.
how_it_makes_money.buyers: Major buyer groups include employers and HR vendors, law firms, property-and-casualty insurers, finance and insurance companies, self-insured employers, government agencies and private individuals.

cost_structure.labor: Labor is the largest cost bucket because case work requires licensed investigators, analysts, researchers, report writers and compliance staff; baseline 2020 wages were $2.393 billion, equal to about 38.0% of 2020 revenue.
cost_structure.technology_and_data: Database subscriptions, court-record access, background-screening platforms, case-management systems, cyber/digital-forensics tools, cameras, GPS-compliant tracking tools and secure storage are a rising 2025-2026 expense category.
cost_structure.insurance_and_compliance: Professional liability coverage, licensing, training, legal review, FCRA procedures, privacy controls and audit trails are material costs because evidence must be lawfully collected and reports must be accurate.
cost_structure.travel_and_field_expense: Surveillance, canvassing, interviews and claims investigations require vehicle, fuel, lodging and equipment costs, though desktop investigations and remote surveillance can reduce field time.
cost_structure.profit: Baseline IBIS profit margin was 5.2% in 2020 and forecast at 7.3% in 2025 as demand recovered and technology lowered some entry and operating costs.

major_players: Command Investigations
CoventBridge Insurance Investigations / CoventBridge Integrity Systems
Pinkerton, part of Securitas
Ethos Risk Services
Lemieux & Associates
DigiStream Investigations
Allied Screening and other background-screening providers
Thousands of local and solo licensed private investigators
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled toward corporate and institutional work rather than classic consumer surveillance alone. Employers still need background and identity verification, insurers are facing more organized and AI-enabled claims fraud, law firms need litigation support, and cyber-enabled scams create demand for OSINT, digital evidence and asset-tracing capabilities. At the same time, the industry is heavily fragmented, with most operators small and local, while insurance-investigation specialists are consolidating to offer national coverage and proprietary technology. Compliance has become a competitive differentiator: FCRA, privacy, adverse-action, data accuracy and state licensing rules make sloppy public-record or algorithmic screening risky.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 insurance SIU, claims surveillance and anti-fraud investigations tied to identity theft, synthetic identity and AI-manipulated evidence
2025-2026 employment background checks, continuous monitoring and credential verification for regulated industries
2025-2026 digital investigations, OSINT, social media research, cyber-enabled fraud support and asset tracing
2025-2026 national accounts for insurers, TPAs, self-insured employers and law firms that want standardized reporting across states
2025-2026 compliance-led screening and investigative reports with stronger audit trails, accuracy checks and adverse-action workflows
whats_shrinking: Traditional domestic infidelity and divorce-linked investigations are structurally pressured by lower divorce-rate trends cited in the baseline outlook
Low-tech local surveillance-only operators face pressure from national providers, better databases, remote surveillance and client procurement consolidation
Informal or weakly documented background-screening practices are shrinking because 2024-2026 FCRA scrutiny raises legal and reputational risk
Routine public-record lookup work is becoming more automated and price-competitive
recent_developments: 2025-01-17: CFPB ordered Equifax to pay a $15 million civil money penalty for credit-reporting and dispute-investigation failures, reinforcing FCRA accuracy risk for consumer-reporting workflows.
2025-01-30: CFPB released its 2025 list of consumer reporting companies, highlighting specialty data used for employment, rental, insurance and other screening decisions.
2025-09-02: NICB projected a 49% rise in insurance fraud linked to identity theft by the end of 2025, including synthetic identity activity in questionable claims.
2025-10-09: Command Investigations acquired Merge Investigations, expanding SIU, web investigation and insurance-defense capabilities.
2026-04-06: FBI reported 2025 IC3 internet crime losses of nearly $21 billion from 1,008,597 complaints, supporting demand for fraud and digital-evidence investigations.
2026-07-07: Command Investigations acquired CoventBridge's insurance division, creating what the company described as the largest US insurance investigations firm.
outlook: Through 2026 and into the late 2020s, private detective services should grow modestly from the 2022 Census benchmark, with better growth in employer screening, insurance fraud, litigation support and digital investigations than in traditional consumer domestic work. BLS projects 6% occupational employment growth from 2024 to 2034, faster than the all-occupation average, but profitability will depend on utilization, investigator availability, data costs, licensing and compliance discipline. The best-positioned firms will combine licensed field capacity with defensible digital research, strong report QA, secure data handling and national account coverage. Small operators can still compete in local surveillance and specialty niches, but broad screening and insurance-investigation work is increasingly won on scale, technology and compliance credibility.
themes: Shift away from divorce-led consumer demand
one_sentence: The US private detective services industry is a fragmented, labor-heavy business-services market where post-pandemic revenue recovery, employment screening, insurance fraud, cyber-enabled scams and legal support work are offset by FCRA/privacy compliance risk and softer traditional divorce-related demand.

title: Private Equity, Hedge Funds & Investment Vehicles in the US
one_liner: Alternative investment funds remain a large, high-margin US finance industry as institutional and private-wealth capital keeps shifting into private equity, hedge funds, private credit, secondaries and evergreen vehicles.
overview: This industry includes private equity funds, hedge funds, closed-end funds, unit investment trusts and other financial vehicles that pool capital and invest in public securities, private companies, credit, derivatives, distressed assets, real assets and other alternatives. The 2022 IBIS baseline put industry revenue at $294.1 billion after 4.0% growth in 2022, with profit of $118.5 billion and a 40.3% profit margin. For 2025, revenue is estimated at about $332.9 billion using the 2022 baseline and the baseline 2022-2027 forecast growth path, while current public data show the asset base has grown faster than revenue: SEC Form PF private funds reported $26.9 trillion in gross assets in 2025Q3, up 10.5% from 2024Q3. Performance and asset growth are concentrated among scaled managers with large distribution platforms, private-credit capabilities, secondaries businesses and access to individual-investor channels.

how_it_makes_money: Funds earn 2025 revenue mainly through recurring management fees on committed capital, net asset value or invested capital, plus performance fees and carried interest when funds exceed hurdle rates or realize gains. Private equity funds also earn transaction, monitoring, capital-solutions and exit-related fees, while hedge funds rely more heavily on management fees, incentive allocations and trading gains. Public alternative managers increasingly add fee-related earnings from private credit, insurance mandates, evergreen vehicles, secondaries and retail-distributed products, which made 2025-2026 revenue less dependent on traditional buyout exits than in earlier cycles.
cost_structure: The industry has a high-profit, talent-heavy cost structure. The 2022 baseline reported $32.8 billion of wages and $118.5 billion of profit, equal to a 40.3% margin. Major 2025-2026 costs include investment-team compensation, carried-interest and bonus accruals, data and trading systems, AI and quant infrastructure, legal and compliance, fund administration, audit and valuation work, investor relations, placement fees, rent, insurance and financing costs inside consolidated funds. Compliance burdens remain meaningful, although the 2026 SEC/CFTC Form PF proposal would reduce reporting obligations for many smaller advisers if finalized.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is expanding but uneven. Hedge funds benefited from volatility, AI-led equity themes and renewed inflows, with HFR reporting $642.8 billion of global hedge fund capital growth in 2025 and a further record jump to $5.6 trillion in 2026Q2. Private equity deal value recovered in 2025, especially at the large-deal end, but exit backlogs and low distributions still pressure LP allocations. Fundraising is increasingly concentrated among scaled managers and specialist strategies, while private wealth, evergreen funds, insurance capital and secondaries are becoming more important sources of growth. Regulation remains fluid after the 2024 court vacatur of SEC private-fund adviser rules and the 2026 SEC/CFTC proposal to streamline Form PF reporting.
whats_growing: Growing segments in 2025-2026 include private credit, infrastructure tied to AI data centers and power demand, continuation vehicles, secondaries, evergreen and tender-offer structures, private-wealth distribution, large-cap buyouts, healthcare and technology hedge fund strategies, event-driven funds, relative-value strategies and operational value-creation programs using AI. SEC Form PF assets grew 10.5% year over year in 2025Q3, and North American private-markets fundraising reached $861 billion in 2025 according to Preqin.
whats_shrinking: Shrinking or pressured areas in 2025-2026 include smaller and undifferentiated managers, traditional closed-end PE fundraising outside North America, underperforming hedge funds, unit investment trusts and closed-end funds relative to newer private-market structures, quick-flip buyout strategies dependent on cheap leverage, and older PE vintages with slow exits. McKinsey reported global closed-end PE fundraising fell 17% in 2025, while smaller funds under $500 million lost share versus funds above $5 billion.

2026-04-24: SEC and CFTC proposed Form PF changes that would raise the filing threshold to $1.0 billion and the large hedge fund adviser reporting threshold to $10.0 billion.

outlook: The outlook for 2026 is positive but more selective than the 2021-era expansion. Revenue should keep growing with asset appreciation, private-wealth inflows, private credit, secondaries and evergreen vehicles, but alpha generation and cash distributions matter more as LPs push for realized returns. Higher financing costs, tighter underwriting, fee pressure and longer holding periods will limit weaker managers. Scaled firms with permanent capital, credit origination, insurance partnerships, AI infrastructure exposure and global fundraising reach are positioned to keep taking share through 2026, while smaller managers need specialization or strong performance to raise successor funds.
